Everything the mind knows about accounting.
Everything the mind knows about technical analysis.
Everything the mind knows about macro and policy.
Everything the mind knows about rates and credit.
Everything the mind knows about options and derivatives.
Everything the mind knows about commodities.
Everything the mind knows about trading and market structure.
Everything the mind knows about risk and portfolios.
Everything the mind knows about statistics and inference.
Everything the mind knows about behavior and bubbles.
Everything the mind knows about games, poker and decisions.
Everything the mind knows about negotiation and haggling.
Everything the mind knows about private markets.
Everything the mind knows about asset management.
Everything the mind knows about the ai buildout.
Everything the mind knows about crypto.
Everything the mind knows about market history.
Everything the mind knows about machine learning.
Everything the mind knows about models and reality.
Everything the mind knows about information edge.
Reading price and volume for trend, momentum, mean reversion and structure; worth only what its signals earn out of sample on the asset in question.
A Japanese trend system: conversion and base lines and a cloud built from 9, 26 and 52-period midpoints, plotted 26 periods ahead.
A trailing stop set a multiple of ATR from the midpoint; the trend flips when the close crosses it.
Wilder's stop-and-reverse level that accelerates toward price as a trend extends.
A volume-weighted RSI on typical price.
Levels at 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% and 78.6% of the last big move, watched as likely pauses; their power is mostly that many traders watch them.
Minervini's stage-two checklist: price above rising 50, 150 and 200-day averages stacked in order, near the 52-week high and well off the low.
A price divided by a benchmark's, against its own average: is it leading or lagging the market.
The average return after a signal or event against all days, with errors that respect overlap; how every technical signal here is judged.
Nine pass-fail tests of profitability, leverage, liquidity and efficiency; high scorers among cheap stocks outperformed in Piotroski (2000).
A weighted sum of balance-sheet and earnings ratios that predicts distress; Z'' is the version for non-manufacturers.
Eight ratios that flag a higher chance of earnings manipulation; above -1.78 is the usual cut-off.
How much of reported profit is cash: cash conversion, accruals, stock pay and capitalized costs.
Revenue growth plus free-cash-flow margin of at least 40% marks a healthy growth company.
Return on equity split into margin times asset turnover times leverage, to see which one is doing the work.
nodes.f: ROE = NI/Sales x Sales/Assets x Assets/Equity

nodes.t: Learning a policy that maximizes reward over time from experience; in sizing, the state is what the market looks like and the action is how much to hold.
Offline reinforcement learning: repeatedly fit the value of each state and action to reward plus the discounted best next value on recorded data.
nodes.f: Q(s,a) = E[r + gamma max Q(s', a')]

nodes.t: Reinforcement learning when actions do not change the next state, as when one investor's trades do not move the market.
Stock and Watson's discounted mean-squared-error weights: models that forecast well recently get more weight.
One interface to every data source the engine reads, with priorities, fallbacks, provenance and a connection check.
Owning the path to the customer: when products are easy to copy, the firm that already reaches billions of users or the enterprise seat wins the new feature.
Ben Thompson's argument that internet winners own the user relationship and commoditize suppliers, so demand, not supply, is the moat.
The users, devices, seats or developers a firm already serves; new AI features ship to them on day one.
Sales reach and channels that turn a product into revenue faster than a rival with a better product can.
Share price divided by earnings per share: how many years of today's profit the price pays for.
Price over the earnings analysts expect for the next twelve months; flattered when forecasts are too high.
Price over the ten-year average of inflation-adjusted earnings (Campbell and Shiller); smooths the cycle and predicts ten-year returns far better than one-year returns.
nodes.f: CAPE = real price / mean(real EPS over 10 years)

nodes.t: The CAPE earnings yield (1/CAPE) minus the real ten-year yield: the extra return stocks offer over inflation-protected bonds.
Earnings per share over price, the inverse of P/E; comparable to a bond yield.
P/E divided by expected growth in percent; Lynch's rough check that a growth company is not overpriced for its growth.
Enterprise value over earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; compares firms with different debt.
Enterprise value over revenue; used when profits are small or distorted.
Price over accounting equity per share; the classic value metric, weaker where assets are intangible.
Annual dividends over price; once a strong predictor of returns, weaker since buybacks replaced dividends.
Dividends plus net buybacks over market value: total cash returned to owners.
Free cash flow over market value; cash, not accounting profit, that the business could hand back.
Buffett's measure: net income plus depreciation minus the capex needed just to keep the business where it is.
Value as the sum of future cash flows, each divided by (1 + discount rate) for every year of waiting.
Solving a DCF backwards: the growth a price already assumes, which can then be checked against how often companies achieve it.
The revenue or earnings growth a price needs to be fair; the engine's main test of irrational pricing.
How often companies of a given size have achieved a given growth rate historically; the outside view on a forecast.
The value of all cash flows after the forecast years; often most of a DCF, which makes long-duration stocks rate sensitive.
The return required to wait for cash; the risk-free rate plus a risk premium.
The blend of the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt, weighted by how the firm is funded.
nodes.f: WACC = E/V re + D/V rd (1 - t)

nodes.t: What shareholders require: the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium in the CAPM.
The extra return investors expect from stocks over safe bonds; low when stocks are expensive relative to yields.
Comparing the stock earnings yield with the ten-year Treasury yield; popular but criticized for mixing a real and a nominal yield (Asness 2003).
Total stock market value over GDP; Buffett's 2001 rough gauge of how expensive the market is.
Market value of firms over the cost of replacing their assets; above one invites building more.
How much investors pay for a unit of profit or cash across the market; high levels mean lower long-run returns on average.
The average return a rational investor anticipates; not a forecast of any one year.
What a business is worth to an owner from its future cash, independent of the quote today.
Buying well below estimated value so errors in the estimate do not cost money (Graham).
After-tax operating profit over the capital tied up to earn it; growth creates value only when ROIC exceeds the cost of capital.
Net income over shareholders' equity; inflated by leverage and buybacks.
A durable advantage (scale, network effects, switching costs, brand, patents) that keeps returns above the cost of capital.
Returns that come from investors paying more per unit of earnings, not from earnings growth; it reverses.
Changes in analysts' forecasts; rising estimates tend to lead prices for a while.
Consensus forecasts of earnings; historically too optimistic a year out.
Net income divided by shares outstanding; buybacks raise it without raising profit.
The rate profits rise; over long periods it tracks nominal GDP for the market as a whole.
Buying assets for less than they are worth on fundamentals (Graham, Buffett, Klarman).
Paying up for companies whose earnings should compound fast for long; works when growth persists.
How sensitive a stock's value is to the discount rate; far-off cash flows mean long duration, like a long bond.
Valuing each business line separately and adding them, often revealing a conglomerate discount.
Market value of equity plus debt minus cash: the price of the whole business.
The tendency of stretched quantities (valuations, margins, volatility) to drift back toward their long-run average.
Dividends over earnings.
A company repurchasing its own stock; returns cash and raises EPS, and is a steady buyer in the market.
Assets minus liabilities on the balance sheet.
The yield on government bills or bonds, the return for waiting without default risk; the base of every discount rate.
The interest rate a company pays to borrow, after the tax saving on interest.
The cash a business would produce if it stopped growing: revenue less costs and the capex needed only to maintain it.
Mauboussin and Rappaport's method: read the expectations a price implies, then judge whether they are likely to be revised.
The rhythm of expansion and recession; earnings, credit and commodity demand all ride it.
A breakdown in funding and trust that forces selling across markets at once.
The slow move by some reserve managers and trade partners away from the dollar, visible mainly in central bank gold buying.
The US Energy Information Administration's weekly inventory data and monthly Short-Term Energy Outlook.
One series moving before another; useful for forecasting only if it survives out of sample.
The exchange of cash and securities after a trade; US stocks settle the next business day.
What an asset earns if prices do not move: a bond's yield over funding, a currency's rate gap, a commodity's roll; it predicts returns across asset classes (Koijen et al. 2018).
Fitting flexible models to data to predict; in markets the signal is weak, the data short and the world changes, so most of the work is validation.
Judging a model on data held out from fitting, repeatedly; in time series the held-out data must come after, and overlapping labels must be purged.
Refitting on an expanding window and forecasting only the next block, as a trader would have.
Dropping training rows whose label window overlaps the test period, plus an embargo after it, so the model cannot peek (Lopez de Prado 2018).
A gap left after each test block before training resumes, against leakage through serial correlation.
Holding out every combination of k of N time blocks, purged; gives many backtest paths and the probability of backtest overfitting.
Training data that contains information from the test period: overlapping labels, revised data, features computed with future values.
Many decision trees on random subsets of rows and features, averaged; robust, but it cannot extrapolate beyond the data (Breiman 2001).
Trees added one at a time, each fitting the previous ensemble's errors (Friedman 2001); powerful and easy to overfit.
Least squares with a penalty on the size of coefficients, which shrinks noisy estimates toward zero.
Penalizing complexity so a model fits signal rather than noise.
Simple models miss real structure; complex ones chase noise; with low signal to noise the simple side usually wins.
Finding the past months most like today and asking what followed; transparent, and only as good as history's resemblance.
Averaging several models; simple averages of forecasts are hard to beat (Rapach, Strauss and Zhou 2010).
Averaging individual predictor forecasts, which beat each one out of sample for the equity premium.
How much a model's held-out error grows when one feature is shuffled; misleading when features substitute for each other.
Which inputs a model relies on; in-sample importance flatters noise, so the engine measures it out of sample.
When today's inputs come from a different distribution than the training data, so the model is extrapolating.
Measuring how far today sits from its nearest historical neighbours, against how far typical months sit from theirs.
Relationships that change over time; the main reason market models decay.
Mean squared error of probability forecasts; the skill score compares it with always forecasting the base rate.
Whether events forecast at 30% happen about 30% of the time.
The chance a model ranks a random positive case above a random negative one; 0.5 is a coin flip.
Whether one forecast's errors are reliably smaller than another's, with errors robust to overlap.
A second model that decides whether to act on a primary model's signal and how big, rather than its direction (Lopez de Prado).
Labelling a trade by which comes first: a profit target, a stop or a time limit.
Asking large language models to read news and predict returns; promising results are hard to separate from look-ahead in their training data.
How much of a series is predictable; for monthly stock returns it is tiny, which is why flexible models overfit.
Loss from decisions based on wrong or misused models (the Fed's SR 11-7 definition, 2011).
Critical review of a model by people with the skill, independence and authority to change it (SR 11-7).
Stating what a model assumes and testing each assumption on the data before trusting the output.
How wrong an assumption can be before the model's conclusion flips: the cost that erases an edge, the correlation that breaks a hedge.
Choosing the decision that stays acceptable over the widest range of errors in the model, instead of the one that is best if the model is right.
Decisions that hold up across many plausible worlds, not just the most likely one.
Alternative histories resampled from the data, in which a decision is re-run to see how often it still holds.
Anomalies earn less after they are published: about 26% lower out of sample and 58% lower after publication (McLean and Pontiff 2016).
Shrinking a backtest's Sharpe ratio for the number of strategies tried; the haircut is larger for modest Sharpes (Harvey and Liu 2015).
Across 888 Quantopian algorithms, backtest Sharpe ratios explained almost none of live performance (Wiecki et al. 2016).
How fat-tailed a variable is in sample-size terms: 0 for the Gaussian, 1 for the Cauchy; it says how much more data the same confidence needs.
Taleb and Douady's test: if losses accelerate as a shock grows, the position is fragile; if they slow, it is antifragile there.
Avoid ruin first; distrust thin-tailed models; prefer convex payoffs; judge by exposure, not forecasts.
For non-perishable things such as ideas or technologies, longer survival so far implies longer expected survival.
Trusting forecasts and advice more when the source bears the cost of being wrong.
Every valuation is a story and numbers; the story must be possible, plausible and probable, and the numbers must follow from it.
Turning a business story into growth, target margin, reinvestment through sales to capital, a cost of capital, terminal growth at most the risk-free rate, and a chance of failure.
Revenue added per dollar of capital invested; sets how much a company must reinvest to grow.
The chance a young or stretched business does not survive, weighed against its value as a going concern.
The return premium that makes the index equal the present value of its expected cash yield, growth and a terminal rate equal to the risk-free rate (Damodaran).
Market-neutral quant funds lost heavily on August 7 to 9, 2007 as crowded positions were unwound (Khandani and Lo).
A deployment error ran old code on one server and lost $460 million in 45 minutes.
Knowing something material before the market prices it, legally: better sources, faster reading, deeper analysis or a different time horizon.
Filings, transcripts, regulators' data and the original papers, read before anyone's summary.
10-Ks, 10-Qs, 8-Ks, proxies and Form 4s on EDGAR; full-text search finds a phrase across every filing.
Form 4 reports of executives' buying and selling; clusters of buying carry more signal than selling.
Data beyond prices and filings: shipping, satellite, card spending, app downloads, job postings, web traffic.
Specialist writers (SemiAnalysis, Stratechery, Doomberg, SixSigma, BowTied Bull) who go deep where sell-side coverage is thin; read for facts and frameworks, check their incentives.
What management says and refuses to say; changes in wording across quarters are a signal.
Treat any tip, thread or newsletter as a lead to check against a primary source, never as the source.
Paid calls with industry practitioners; useful for context, a legal risk near material non-public information.
Sales recognized in the period; the top line every margin is measured against.
The rules for when a sale counts as revenue; aggressive timing pulls future sales forward.
Revenue minus the direct cost of goods, over revenue; pricing power shows up here first.
Operating income over revenue.
Net income over revenue.
How much profit rises for a rise in sales when costs are fixed; cuts both ways.
Revenue, costs and profit over a period.
What a company owns and owes at a point in time.
Cash from operations, investing and financing; harder to flatter than earnings.
Cash generated by the business in the period, before investment.
Operating cash flow minus capital spending: cash left for owners.
Spending on long-lived assets such as data centres, fabs and power plants.
The spending needed just to keep capacity where it is; often approximated by depreciation.
Spreading an asset's cost over its useful life; a short life lowers profits now, a long one flatters them.
The years over which an asset is depreciated; servers set at five to six years when the economic life may be shorter.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; ignores the cost of the assets that earn it.
EBITDA with management's chosen exclusions; read the adjustments.
Earnings that exclude items management calls unusual, often including stock pay; higher than GAAP by design.
US Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the audited standard.
Pay in shares; a real cost to owners through dilution even though it uses no cash.
Earnings not yet backed by cash; high accruals predict lower future returns (Sloan 1996).
Operating cash flow over net income; below one means profits are not turning into cash.
How well reported profit reflects durable cash generation.
Receivables and inventory minus payables; swings in it move cash without moving profit.
Cash collected before the service is delivered; flatters cash flow while it grows.
Goods held for sale; a build-up can signal weak demand or a coming price war.
The premium paid in an acquisition over the fair value of net assets; written down when the deal sours.
A write-down when an asset is worth less than its book value.
Debt minus cash.
Net debt over EBITDA, a lender's first measure of how stretched a borrower is.
Operating income over interest expense.
Long-term rental commitments, now on the balance sheet; data-centre leases are large and long.
Obligations kept outside the reported balance sheet through vehicles or guarantees.
The average of the last n prices, updated each period; smooths noise to show the trend.
An equal-weighted moving average.
A moving average that weights recent prices more, with weight 2/(n+1) on the newest.
The average of the last 200 trading days (about ten months); price above it is the most common definition of an uptrend.
The average of the last 50 trading days; the medium-term trend.
Hold stocks when the monthly price is above its ten-month average, else cash (Faber 2007); the engine tests it on 155 years.
The 50-day average crossing above (golden) or below (death) the 200-day.
Wilder's 0 to 100 gauge of recent gains against losses over 14 periods; above 70 is called overbought, below 30 oversold.
Labels for prices that have risen or fallen fast; on their own they rarely predict reversals in trending markets.
Appel's moving average convergence divergence: the 12-period EMA minus the 26-period EMA, against its own 9-period EMA.
A 20-period average with bands two standard deviations above and below; band width tracks volatility.
Wilder's measure of daily range including gaps; used to size stops.
Wilder's average directional index: trend strength, not direction.
Where the close sits within the recent high-low range, 0 to 100.
A running total of volume signed by the day's direction.
Volume-weighted average price over a session; an execution benchmark as much as an indicator.
Shares or contracts traded; conviction behind a move.
Price levels where buying or selling has gathered before; self-fulfilling when many watch them.
A move through support or resistance or to a new high.
The year's extreme prices; stocks near highs tend to keep doing better (George and Hwang 2004).
Buying what has risen and selling what has fallen over months, across many markets; paid in crises (Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen 2017).
The tendency of recent winners to keep winning for months (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993).
An asset's own past year return predicting its next month (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012).
Trend followers' habit of making money in long sell-offs.
Price making a new high while an oscillator does not; a warning, not a signal.
How many stocks share in a move; narrow rallies led by a few giants are fragile.
Running total of advancing minus declining stocks.
A breadth gauge of the trend under the index surface.
Put volume over call volume; extremes read as fear or greed.
Levels at 38.2, 50 and 61.8 percent of a move; widely used, without reliable evidence.
The fall from the previous peak; the loss that tests whether an investor can stay invested.
Finding a rule that worked by trying many; its backtest overstates its future (Sullivan, Timmermann and White 1999).
The rise in the general price level; erodes cash and bonds and decides what the Fed does.
The BLS index of consumer prices; the headline inflation measure.
Inflation without food and energy; the Fed's guide to the trend.
The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
The overnight rate the central bank sets (the fed funds rate in the US).
A guide that sets the policy rate from inflation's gap to target and output's gap to potential.
How far the economy runs above or below its potential.
Central bank bond buying to push down long rates and add reserves.
Letting the central bank's bonds roll off; drains reserves.
The ease of funding and trading; ample liquidity props up risk assets, scarce liquidity breaks them.
Banks' deposits at the Fed; the system's cash.
Where money funds park cash at the Fed; once it is empty, drains come out of reserves.
An index of how easy credit, equity and dollar conditions are (Chicago Fed NFCI).
The value of everything an economy produces; nominal GDP growth bounds long-run profit growth.
A broad, lasting fall in activity; earnings fall, defaults rise, and stocks typically drop a third.
Inflation falling without a recession.
High inflation with weak growth; the worst regime for a stock and bond portfolio.
The share of the labour force without work.
A recession signal when the three-month average unemployment rate rises half a point above its prior-year low.
Monthly US job gains; the market's most-watched data release.
Government spending above revenue; financed by issuing bonds.
The stock of bonds a government owes; its interest cost rises with rates.
The amount of new duration the market must absorb, from Treasuries and corporate issuers.
The world's reserve and funding currency; a strong dollar tightens global conditions and weighs on commodities and gold.
Taxes on imports; raise prices and can lower growth.
Output per hour; the only lasting source of higher real wages and margins.
The rise in pay; feeds services inflation.
Cash and deposits in the economy.
A sudden jump in oil prices from lost supply; raises inflation and lowers growth.
Currencies' prices against each other; set by rate gaps, growth, flows and risk appetite.
Borrowing in a low-rate currency to hold a high-rate one; earns slowly and loses fast in crises.
The benchmark long-term rate; it sets mortgage rates and the discount rate on long-duration stocks.
Yields on bills and two-year notes; follow expected policy rates.
Yields by maturity; its slope reflects expected policy and the term premium.
Short rates above long rates; historically preceded most US recessions with a long, variable lag.
Trades on the curve's slope widening or narrowing.
The extra yield for locking money up long instead of rolling short bills; rises with supply and inflation uncertainty.
The yield after inflation, observed on TIPS; the true cost of money.
Nominal yield minus the TIPS yield: the inflation the bond market prices.
Treasury bonds whose principal rises with CPI.
The percentage change in a bond's price for a one-point change in yield; long bonds have high duration.
How duration itself changes with yield; long bonds gain more when yields fall than they lose when they rise.
Moves opposite the yield.
An ETF of 20+ year Treasuries; the book's classic hedge, which fails when stocks and bonds fall together.
What a bond earns if yields do not move: its coupon over funding plus the price gain as it rolls down the curve.
The extra yield on corporate debt over Treasuries; widens before and during stress.
Bonds rated below investment grade; behave half like stocks.
The weakest rated borrowers; cracks show here first.
Bonds rated BBB- or better.
Failure to pay; default rates rise in recessions and when rates stay high for borrowers who refinance.
What creditors get back after a default.
Insurance against a borrower's default, quoted as an annual spread.
Investors who sell government bonds to punish fiscal excess, pushing yields up.
Implied volatility of Treasury options; the VIX of bonds.
The gap between swap rates and Treasury yields; negative when dealers' balance sheets are full.
How new debt is sold; weak demand (tails, low bid-to-cover) moves yields.
The right, not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) at a set price before a date.
The right to buy at the strike; pays when the price rises above it.
The right to sell at the strike; insurance against a fall.
Buying one put and selling a lower one: cheaper insurance that stops paying below the lower strike.
Buying a put and selling a call: free or cheap protection that gives up gains above the call.
Selling calls against stock held: income that caps upside.
Buying (or selling) both a call and a put: a bet on (or against) a big move.
The 1973 formula that prices a European option from spot, strike, time, rates and volatility.
nodes.f: C = S N(d1) - K e^(-rT) N(d2)

nodes.t: The volatility that makes the option price fit Black-Scholes; the market's priced uncertainty.
The volatility prices actually showed; usually below implied, which pays option sellers on average.
Implied minus realized variance; the insurance premium option sellers collect, and lose in crashes.
Downside puts priced at higher implied volatility than calls: crash insurance demand.
Cboe's 30-day implied volatility of the S&P 500; the fear gauge.
Option sensitivities: delta (to price), gamma (delta's change), vega (to volatility), theta (to time), rho (to rates).
How much dealers must buy or sell as prices move to stay hedged; negative gamma amplifies moves.
Options expiring the same day; now a large share of S&P 500 option volume.
Call minus put equals spot minus the discounted strike; arbitrage keeps them aligned.
Exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell later at a price agreed now, marked to market daily.
A private agreement to trade later at a set price.
Spot minus futures; converges to zero at expiry.
Collateral posted against a leveraged position; margin calls force selling in falls.
A position that gains when the main bet loses; it costs something on average.
Cheap, far out-of-the-money protection that pays only in crashes (Spitznagel, Taleb).
Raw materials traded in bulk: energy, metals, grains, softs and livestock.
How most investors hold commodities; returns come from spot, roll and collateral (Gorton and Rouwenhorst 2006).
Futures above spot, usually when inventories are ample; rolling long positions loses money.
Futures below spot, usually when supply is tight; long positions earn as they roll.
The gain or loss from replacing an expiring future with the next; positive in backwardation.
The benefit of holding the physical commodity when supply is short (Kaldor, Working).
Futures equal spot plus financing and storage minus convenience yield; low inventories mean backwardation.
Financing plus storage costs of holding a commodity until a future date.
Keynes's idea that hedgers pay speculators a premium, so futures sit below the expected spot price.
Stocks of oil, gas, metals or grain; the buffer that sets the curve's shape.
The producers' group that sets output quotas; its spare capacity caps price spikes.
Production that can be added quickly; low spare capacity makes prices jumpy.
The US government's emergency oil stock.
The North Sea benchmark for most of the world's oil.
The US benchmark, delivered at Cushing, Oklahoma.
The gap between the two benchmarks; cointegrated, with deviations that close over weeks.
The refining margin: product prices minus crude.
Soybean meal and oil value minus soybean cost: the crusher's margin.
Power price minus the gas cost to make it: the gas plant's margin.
Henry Hub in the US, TTF in Europe, LNG in Asia; strongly seasonal and storage driven.
Gas cooled to liquid and shipped; links regional gas markets, a fifth of it through Hormuz.
A store of value with no yield; driven by real yields, the dollar, fear and central bank buying.
Reserve managers buying gold to diversify away from dollars; a steady bid since 2022.
Half precious metal, half industrial input.
The industrial metal of wiring and grids; Dr. Copper for its read on growth, and a data-centre input.
Currencies of exporters (AUD, CAD, NOK, BRL, ZAR) that move with their commodities.
Steel's raw material; China's construction cycle sets its price.
China consumes about half the world's metals; its credit cycle drives the metals cycle.
Wheat, corn, soybeans and their oils; weather and stocks-to-use drive prices.
The USDA's monthly world supply and demand estimates for crops.
Coffee, cocoa, sugar, cotton: tropical crops prone to weather shocks.
The CFTC's weekly breakdown of futures positions by trader type; extremes in speculators' positions mark crowded trades.
The old saying that stocks do better from November to April than from May to October; the engine tests it since 1871 and since 1950.
Regular calendar patterns: gas peaks in winter, grains around harvest; in stocks, mostly folklore.
A decade-long price boom from a demand surge meeting slow supply.
The shift to electricity and renewables; raises demand for copper, power and gas backup.
The chokepoint for about a fifth of world oil and LNG; its closure in 2026 is the book's live oil shock.
The gap between the best buy and sell quotes; the toll for immediacy.
How much can trade without moving the price; vanishes when needed most.
Resting limit orders at each price.
An order to trade only at a set price or better; may not fill.
An order to trade now at the best available price; certain fill, uncertain price.
An order that becomes a market order when a price is hit; can fill far away in a gap.
The difference between the expected and actual fill price.
How much a trade moves the price against itself; grows with the square root of size (the square-root law).
Impact scales with the square root of the order's share of daily volume, across markets.
Trading a large order fast (more impact) or slow (more price risk) optimally (2000).
Turning a decision into fills at low cost: slicing, timing, venue choice.
Time-weighted average price: an even pace of trading.
The cost from decision price to final fill, including what never filled.
How far price moves per unit of order flow when informed traders hide among noise traders (Kyle 1985).
Trading against someone who knows more; the reason spreads exist (Glosten and Milgrom 1985).
A dealer who quotes both sides and earns the spread while managing inventory and adverse selection.
A dealer's exposure to positions accumulated while making markets.
Automated trading at microsecond speed, mostly market making and arbitrage.
Delay between a signal and an order reaching the market.
Wholesalers paying brokers for retail orders, which they fill inside the spread.
Venues without public quotes; a large share of US volume trades off exchange.
A large trade negotiated privately and printed at once, often at a discount.
Borrowing shares to sell, hoping to buy back cheaper; losses are unbounded.
Shorts forced to buy as prices rise, driving prices higher.
The fee to borrow shares to short.
A demand for more collateral; forced selling begets more selling.
Borrowing to hold more than one's capital; magnifies gains, losses and the risk of being forced out.
Cutting positions to reduce leverage, often all at once.
Exchange-wide trading halts after large falls.
US stocks settle one business day after trade since 2024.
Authorized participants swap baskets for ETF shares, keeping prices near NAV.
Forced buying and selling when index weights change.
Individual investors' share of trading; surges in manias.
Profiting from a price gap between equivalent assets; limited by capital and risk (Shleifer and Vishny 1997).
Commissions, spreads, impact and taxes; they turn many backtested edges negative.
How much of a portfolio trades each year.
The standard deviation of returns; the most common, and incomplete, measure of risk.
How much an asset moves with the market; the CAPM's measure of risk that cannot be diversified away.
Return beyond what the asset's risk exposures explain; mostly luck after costs (Fama and French 2010).
Sharpe's 1964 model: expected return rises only with beta.
How two returns move together, from -1 to 1; it rises in crises, when diversification is needed most.
Positive when inflation drives both; then bonds stop hedging stocks.
How often assets crash together; correlation understates it.
Holding assets that do not move together to lower risk without lowering expected return.
Too much in one name, sector or factor; the AI book's defining risk.

The average loss beyond the VaR; describes the tail.
Extreme moves far more often than a bell curve allows; kurtosis above 3.
A rare, extreme, unforeseen event that is explained only afterwards (Taleb).

The chance of losing the whole bankroll; falls exponentially with bankroll over variance.
How much to put in each bet; more important than which bets.
A rule to exit after a set loss; limits damage, adds whipsaw.
Returning weights to target; sells winners and buys losers.
Weighting assets so each adds equal risk, usually with leverage on bonds (Bridgewater's All Weather).
60% stocks and 40% bonds; it suffered its worst year in 2022 as both fell.
How much hedge per unit of exposure; the minimum-variance ratio is the regression slope.
Tilting toward characteristics with long-run premia: value, momentum, quality, size, low volatility, carry.
Cheap stocks beating expensive ones over long periods; it suffered a lost decade to 2020.
Profitable, stable, low-debt companies earning more than their risk suggests.
Low-risk stocks earning as much as high-risk ones.
The book's loss in a chosen bad scenario.
Weighing a few coherent futures instead of one forecast.
Many funds in the same trade; exits become stampedes.
A period with its own rules (low inflation, high inflation, crisis); links and hedges change between them.
Active return over tracking error.
Fitting a line (or plane) through data to measure how one variable moves with others.
The regression that minimizes squared errors.
The share of variation a model explains in-sample; flattering.

The chance of a result at least this extreme if nothing were going on; not the chance the idea is wrong.

How much an estimate would vary across samples.

A step-down correction that controls the chance of any false positive.
The expected share of false findings among those declared (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995).
A model that fits noise; great in-sample, poor after.
How often the in-sample winner falls to the bottom half out of sample (Bailey et al. 2017).

Judging a model only on data it was not built on.
Using information in a backtest that was not available at the time.
Studying only what survived (funds, stocks) and so overstating returns.

A series whose statistical behaviour does not drift; prices are not, returns roughly are.

Shocks spreading across markets beyond what fundamentals justify.
Estimating which variables are linked once all others are held fixed, with most links set to zero.
Correlation after removing what other variables explain.
Keeping only what survives refits on many half-samples, with a bound on false findings.
Tracking a hidden quantity that drifts, updating with each observation.

Answering by simulating many random worlds.
Revising a belief in proportion to how much more likely the evidence is under it than under the alternative.

Combining rival models with the weights that forecast best out of sample.

How heavy the tails are; 3 for a bell curve.

Ignoring how common something is in general when judging a specific case.

Estimates pulled toward an arbitrary starting number (Tversky and Kahneman 1974).

Seeking evidence that agrees with what one already believes.

Believing after the fact that one saw it coming.
Fitting a tidy story to random events.
Believing a run must reverse.
Staying in because of what has already been spent.

Buffett's advice to be fearful when others are greedy and the reverse.
Shares bid up by online retail crowds and short squeezes (2021).
Cheap, volatile shares overpriced for their small chance of a huge gain.
Believing skill governs what chance governs.

Evidence written down in advance that would reverse a decision.
Judging a case by the base rate of similar cases before its details.
The group of similar past cases used for a base rate.

How widely results scatter around expected value; short runs are dominated by it.

Pot odds including what can be won on later streets if the draw hits.
A hand's share of the pot on average against the opponents' range; the engine simulates it.
All the hands an opponent could have given their actions; think in ranges, not single hands.
The value of a bet from the chance opponents fold.
Betting a weak hand so a stronger one folds; in equilibrium, bluffs keep bets credible.
Acting last, with more information; worth money in poker and in markets.
Unintended signals of strength or weakness.
Emotional decision-making after losses; the trader's version is revenge trading.
Keeping each bet small relative to capital so variance cannot end the game.
An unexploitable strategy, a Nash equilibrium; limit hold'em heads-up was solved in 2015 (Bowling et al.).
Deviating from equilibrium to profit from an opponent's mistakes, at the risk of being exploited back.
A set of strategies where no player gains by changing alone.
Randomizing between actions so an opponent cannot predict and exploit.
Each does better defecting whatever the other does, yet both do worse than if they cooperated; the AI capex race.
Hyperscalers each spending more because the others do, even if all would earn more spending less.
Coordination under noisy private information: when a crowded trade runs (Morris and Shin).
Depositors withdrawing because they fear others will; gates in private credit are a run's brakes.
One side knowing more; prices, spreads and contracts adjust for it.
Costly actions that reveal private information (dividends, buybacks, insider buying).
Winning an auction often means having overestimated the value.
A price set by competing bids: English, Dutch, sealed-bid; Treasuries and IPOs are auctioned.
Laying out choices, chance events and payoffs to compute the best path.
How much a piece of information would raise the expected value of a decision before it is known.
Judging decisions by their process and odds, not by how one outcome turned out (Duke).
Judging a decision by its outcome alone.
Whether the average over many people equals one person's average over time; leverage breaks it.

The worst price at which one would still deal.
Zone of possible agreement: the gap between the buyer's and seller's reservation prices.

Shrinking concessions signal approaching a limit.
Alternating offers over a shrinking pie: the more patient side gets more (Rubinstein 1982).

Trading concessions on issues each side values differently to create value.

Quarterly Review and Outlook (firm publication; Van Hoisington and Lacy Hunt's team)

R* and inflationary expectations suggest the rally in long Treasury bonds will continue through 2024, with the strong prospect for an even longer horizon for this trend. Low neutral rates and falling inflation expectations point to a multi-year rally in long Treasuries. long Treasuries bond rally neutral rate yields fall
Founder, Vanguard Group
Don't look for the needle in the haystack. Just buy the haystack! Stop trying to pick winners and simply own the whole market through an index fund. index fund haystack stock picking passive

My advice to the trustee could not be more simple: Put 10% of the cash in short-term government bonds and 90% in a very low-cost S&P 500 index fund. For his own heirs, Buffett prescribes a cheap S&P 500 index fund rather than picking stocks or managers. index fund S&P 500 90/10 low cost

I saw that with 15 to 20 good, uncorrelated return streams, I could dramatically reduce my risks without reducing expected returns. Combining many uncorrelated bets cuts risk without giving up return, the closest thing to a free lunch. holy grail uncorrelated diversification risk reduction

That trust helps businesses raise the capital they need to grow, and it allows families to spread their investments across many assets at low cost instead of relying on just one. Cheap, broad diversification across many assets is a core benefit that fair markets give ordinary families. diversification low cost families capital markets

A well-diversified portfolio would have somewhere between 10% and 15% in the portfolio of gold. Proper diversification means holding assets beyond stocks and bonds, including a meaningful slice of gold. diversification gold asset allocation portfolio
Senior Vice President, Portfolio Manager, Research, Acadian Asset Management

Much of the discourse about passive investing is simply misguided. Fears that index funds are distorting or breaking markets are mostly wrong. passive investing index funds market efficiency defense of indexing
Founder and CEO, Fundsmith

If you want an index fund, you can buy one with much lower costs than we or any other active investment manager apply. An active fund should not mimic the index; investors who want the index should simply buy a cheap one. active vs passive index fund fees Magnificent Seven

And now some people can't tell their best ideas from their worst. Concentrating in your best ideas only works if you can actually tell which ideas are your best. best ideas concentration self-knowledge overconfidence

Passive investors have no opinion about value. Index money buys regardless of price, which leaves mispricings for stock pickers and weakens markets. passive investing index funds price discovery active management

And now passive investing has removed price discovery from the equity markets. Index fund flows ignore fundamentals, inflating a bubble in passive investing that will end badly. index bubble passive investing price discovery Burry

One's knowledge and experience are definitely limited and there are seldom more than two or three enterprises at any given time in which I personally feel myself entitled to put full confidence. Only a few companies at a time deserve full confidence, so put real size into those rather than spreading thin. concentration conviction Keynes know what you own

On the other hand, if you are a know-something investor, able to understand business economics and to find five to ten sensibly-priced companies that possess important long-term competitive advantages, conventional diversification makes no sense for you. An investor who truly understands businesses should own a handful of great ones, not a diversified basket. concentration know-something investor five to ten stocks diversification

I think diversification and all the stuff they're teaching at business school today is probably the most misguided concept everywhere. Textbook diversification is wrong; great investors make big, concentrated bets. diversification concentration business school conviction

The wise ones bet heavily when the world offers them that opportunity. They bet big when they have the odds. And the rest of the time, they don't. Wait for rare high-odds opportunities and then bet big on them instead of spreading money around. bet big concentration odds patience

History tells us that leverage all too often produces zeroes, even when it is employed by very smart people. Borrowed money can wipe out even brilliant investors, so avoid leverage. leverage debt ruin Berkshire
Scientific adviser, Universa Investments
You wouldn't drive a car without insurance. A large portfolio should always carry crash insurance; dropping tail hedges is reckless. tail hedging insurance black swan CalPERS

But levered portfolios face a downside risk to which there isn't a corresponding upside: the risk of ruin. Leverage magnifies both ways, but it adds a one-sided danger of being wiped out. leverage risk of ruin debt downside

I probably shouldn't say this, but when you see one cockroach, there are probably more. Early credit losses usually signal more hidden risk, so stay defensive on leveraged lending. credit risk private credit leverage warning signs
Founder and CIO, Universa Investments

The goal of risk mitigation, like the goal of investing, should be to raise our rate of compounding over time. Good crash protection should raise long-run compound returns, not just reduce volatility. tail hedging safe haven compounding risk mitigation

You shouldn't expect to make money without bearing risk, but you shouldn't expect to make money just for taking risk. Risk is necessary for returns, but taking risk alone does not guarantee being paid for it. risk premium risk taking returns risk control
Founder, Soros Fund Management

One of the hardest things to judge is what level of risk is safe. Sizing risk correctly is genuinely hard, cutting both ways between too much and too little. position sizing risk judgment Soros leverage

Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses, whether controlled or only partially owned. Despite a big cash pile, owning businesses and bearing equity risk beats sitting safely in cash. cash equities risk taking Berkshire
Chief Investment Officer, CalPERS

We terminated explicit tail-risk hedging options strategies because of their high cost, lack of scalability, and the fact that there are better alternatives available to CalPERS. Explicit tail hedges cost too much and do not scale, so a big fund is better off without them. tail hedging cost of hedging CalPERS pension
There is no way one could produce results like ours without ups and downs. Outsized returns require accepting big swings rather than smoothing them away. volatility drawdowns returns Soros

I strongly believe the only way to make long-term returns in our business that are superior is by being a pig. Superior returns come from betting very big when you have conviction. pig position sizing aggressive conviction

As far as Soros is concerned, when you're right on something, you can't own enough. When a trade is right, press it as hard as possible instead of playing it safe. position sizing Soros go for the jugular conviction

Our goal is to build more intelligent leverage to benefit our common stock shareholders. Borrowing more to buy bitcoin is a deliberate way to boost returns for shareholders. leverage bitcoin convertible bonds MicroStrategy
Founder and CEO, Baupost Group

People who chase growth, who chase high fliers, inevitably lose because they paid a premium price. Paying up for hot growth stocks is a losing game; buy bargains instead. growth stocks premium price value investing high fliers

A great company that gets expensive is much worse than a bad company that's really cheap, so you have to look at pricing. Price matters more than quality: an overpriced great company is a worse bet than a cheap bad one. valuation great company cheap stocks price

Buying such an issue is like betting on a topheavy favorite in a horse race. Stocks with obviously bright prospects already price them in, so buying them offers poor odds. growth stocks priced in margin of safety Graham
Good investing doesn't come from buying good things, but from buying things well. Returns depend on the price you pay, not on how good the company is. valuation bubble price paid quality

If you're going to play the cheap game, you've got to make sure, it is armor-plated with as much quality as you can get into it. Buy cheap, but insist on quality so the bargain is not a value trap. cheap stocks quality value trap bubble

We think the very term 'value investing' is redundant. What is 'investing' if it is not the act of seeking value at least sufficient to justify the amount paid? The value versus growth split is false; all investing is paying less than what something is worth. value vs growth redundant intrinsic value Buffett

A good investment is one in which the price is right for what the value turns out to be. Neither cheap nor expensive is good in itself; what matters is price relative to eventual value. price vs value valuation Magnificent Seven intrinsic value

Some of the highest quality businesses in the world are trading at extremely cheap prices. The best setup is owning top-quality businesses when they briefly trade cheap. quality cheap buy the dip great businesses

It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price. Paying a fair price for an excellent business beats buying a mediocre one cheaply. wonderful company fair price quality cigar butt

But now that you control Berkshire, add to it wonderful businesses purchased at fair prices and give up buying fair businesses at wonderful prices. Munger pushed Buffett away from cheap mediocre businesses toward great businesses at fair prices. wonderful businesses fair price Munger quality

In my business a fourbagger is nice, but a tenbagger is the fiscal equivalent of two home runs and a double. The big wins come from stocks that grow tenfold, so hunt for growth stories with that upside. tenbagger growth stocks upside Lynch

Conversely, if a business earns 18% on capital over 20 or 30 years, even if you pay an expensive looking price, you'll end up with a fine result. Over long horizons a high-return business rewards you even if you paid a price that looked expensive. return on capital quality compounders paying up long term

What they have in their portfolios are more value traps than they now realize, if we're right on our research. Disruptive innovation is turning cheap traditional stocks into value traps, so own the disruptors instead. value traps disruptive innovation growth ARK

The next big crisis in the financial markets, it's going to be private credit. Gundlach names private credit, not AI, as the source of the next major financial crisis. crisis private credit subprime garbage lending
Founder and CIO, Saba Capital Management
I think we are in the super-early innings of the wheels coming off the car. Weinstein says the unraveling of private credit funds has only just begun. redemptions blowup BDCs Blue Owl

When you see one cockroach, there are probably more, and so everyone should be forewarned of this one. Dimon warns that the first credit blowups likely signal more hidden problems to come. cockroaches Tricolor First Brands credit cycle

The worst of loans are made in the best of times. Marks argues that a long credit boom loosens standards, so the loans now coming to light were made carelessly. lending standards credit cycle cockroaches complacency

It's a classic contagion phenomenon: 'If you can't sell what you want, you sell what you can.' El-Erian warns that redemption gates in private credit can force investors to dump healthy assets elsewhere. contagion liquidity redemptions gates

Many know that in PE they're getting some serious smoothing, and a palatable (as it's way understated) reported volatility. Asness says private market marks understate true volatility, which investors knowingly accept. marks volatility laundering smoothing illiquidity

We have seen a number of proposals from private equity funds where the returns are really not calculated in a manner that I would regard as honest. Buffett says private fund return figures are presented in ways he considers misleading. marks returns private equity honesty

If I were running a pension fund, I would be very careful about what was being offered to me. Buffett advises institutions to be skeptical of private fund pitches. pensions private equity due diligence returns

I don't think today's issues are systemic in the sense that there's something wrong with the lending system. Marks says recent credit losses reflect recurring behavior in booms, not a broken lending system. systemic risk cockroaches credit cycle fraud
I don't expect it to be systemic, but I do expect there to be problems. Dimon expects losses in private credit but not a system-wide crisis. systemic risk retail investors ratings hell to pay
President and COO, Blackstone
I still think it's a very good time for private credit. Gray says the opportunity in private credit remains attractive despite the cockroach scare. opportunity Blackstone returns asset class

We believe that private markets offer the potential to enhance retirement outcomes for participants Fink argues private markets belong in ordinary retirement portfolios. retirement democratization 401k private markets
CEO, Apollo Global Management
The vast, vast majority of private credit is investment grade. Rowan says private credit is mostly high-quality lending, not risky leveraged loans. investment grade safety banks definition

Lenders and bargain hunters face much better prospects in this changed environment than they did in 2009-21. Marks argues higher rates have made lending and credit far more attractive than in the zero-rate era. sea change higher rates credit returns lenders

People have really just lost their minds, and the headlines get more and more hysterical and have almost nothing to do with the substance. Rowan dismisses private credit fears as media hysteria unconnected to fundamentals. hysteria fears overblown insurance Apollo
Chairman, CEO and Co-founder, Blackstone

Our default rate on these types of loans is three tenths of 1%. I don't know if there's a bank around that has a default rate that's lower. Schwarzman says Blackstone's private loans default less than bank loans. default rate safety banks Blackstone
Pouring billions of dollars into China now is a tragic mistake. Soros says investing large sums in China is a losing and dangerous bet. uninvestable geopolitics BlackRock Xi

The property crash in China will be worse than it was in America or the UK. Chanos predicts China's property bust will exceed the US and UK housing crashes. property bubble short seller debt real estate

No one knows how far the pendulum will swing back toward the more Maoist/Marxist ways of doing things. Dalio flags the policy risk that China drifts back toward state control. policy risk lost decade debt Xi
Founder and CIO, Hayman Capital Management

You have to say, each country run by maybe a despotic authoritarian should be re-reviewed and maybe not invested in. Bass argues authoritarian markets such as China deserve to be reassessed or avoided. uninvestable authoritarian geopolitics Russia
I didn't stop to realize they're still a goddamn retailer. Munger admits his Alibaba bet underrated how competitive Chinese internet retail is. Alibaba mistake competition Chinese tech
I have not sold anything in China yet, but I'm asking questions. After a strong run, Rogers is holding his China shares but questioning whether to trim. China rally holding valuation Rogers

I can't diversify as well as I'd like to without investing in China. Dalio says China is a necessary part of a well-diversified portfolio despite its risks. diversification China contrarian Bridgewater
I'm not giving up investing in China. Rogers remains a committed long-term investor in China. long term China conviction Rogers
So naturally, I'm willing to have some China risk in the Munger portfolio. Munger accepts China exposure because he sees better companies at lower prices. BYD value China risk Munger

I think it is excellent time - if you haven't been in emerging market bonds or high-yield bonds - to contemplate at least a partial shift based upon the level of the dollar and valuation. Gundlach says valuations and the dollar make it a good time to rotate into emerging market debt. emerging markets EM bonds dollar valuation
I hope that the Chinese market collapses so I can buy Chinese shares. Rogers welcomes a Chinese selloff as a chance to buy more. contrarian buy the dip China slowdown
Founder and President, Appaloosa Management
Everything. ETFs, I would do futures - everything. Everything. Tepper says to buy every kind of China exposure after Beijing's stimulus. buy everything stimulus Alibaba ETFs

The leading companies of China are stronger and better than practically any other leading companies anywhere, and they're available at a much cheaper price. Munger says China's top companies are world class and much cheaper than peers. value cheap quality China

No one knows what oil prices will do over the next month, year, or decade. Buffett refuses to forecast oil prices even while holding a large Occidental stake. oil price forecasting Occidental humility

We particularly like its vast oil and gas holdings in the United States, as well as its leadership in carbon-capture initiatives, though the economic feasibility of this technique has yet to be proven. Buffett values Occidental for its large US oil and gas reserves. Occidental reserves US shale Berkshire

But Vicki does know how to separate oil from rock, and that's an uncommon talent, valuable to her shareholders and to her country. Buffett backs Occidental on the strength of its operator rather than an oil price call. Occidental management energy stocks Berkshire

Meeting rising demand will require expanding supply across oil and gas, renewables, storage, nuclear, and grids. Fink says rising energy demand requires more oil and gas supply alongside other sources. energy pragmatism supply demand all of the above
Natural gas remains essential for reliability, and the U.S. has abundant supply. Fink calls gas indispensable but notes US supply is plentiful. natural gas reliability supply power demand

America should lead the way in generating more energy to meet greater demand, including from AI, which will require huge amounts of energy. Dimon argues AI-driven demand calls for a large expansion of US energy production. AI energy demand production policy

The world still needs oil and natural gas today, but not all hydrocarbons are equal when it comes to their carbon footprint. Dimon says oil and gas remain necessary while favoring lower-carbon fuels. energy security transition hydrocarbons Ukraine

Statistically, also, the level of price rises makes it extremely unlikely that the old trend is still in place. Grantham argues the century-long decline in commodity prices, oil included, has ended for good. commodities scarcity paradigm shift resources

In our view, oil prices are on the threshold of a significant decline. Wood argues the war-driven oil spike is near its end and prices are set to fall sharply. oil price decline deflation Iran war demand destruction

Based on the pent-up supply built up behind the Strait of Hormuz, oil prices could drop precipitously once peace breaks out and the Strait opens. Supply bottled up behind Hormuz would flood the market once the strait reopens, crushing prices. Strait of Hormuz glut oil crash supply

The key lesson here may be that cartels and other anti-market mechanisms can’t hold forever. OPEC-style price support eventually breaks, so propped-up oil prices can collapse. OPEC cartel 2014 oil crash price support
Managing Member and Portfolio Manager, Masters Capital Management

In this testimony I will explain that Institutional Investors are one of, if not the primary, factors affecting commodities prices today. A hedge fund manager argued the 2008 oil spike was inflated by index speculators rather than fundamentals. speculation 2008 oil bubble index funds commodities
Managing partners, Goehring & Rozencwajg Associates

Evidence that energy may be the cheapest major asset class in the world. The resource investors argue energy is deeply undervalued after years of capital starvation. underinvestment energy stocks valuation supply shock
The accounting stress test from the 2026 field manual, as pure functions the page mirrors exactly.

The reality check: every model in the engine states its assumptions, the data test each one, and each conclusion is re-run in worlds where the assumption fails. A portfolio manager's complaint about quants is that the assumptions that make a model tractable (normal returns, independent months, stable parameters, stable correlations, no costs, known parameters, no crowding) are the ones the market breaks; this module
The atlas: the brain grown from 6 measured series to every monthly series the engine can read, with its structure learned from the data instead of drawn by hand.
The brain: measured links between the parts of the financial system, by regime.

How far to trust the brain: honest error bars, a stacked ensemble of world models, and what it would take for an unseen cause to erase a measured link. Python is canonical; the page renders the result (brain.json or snap12.js).
The field manual's engine work: regime and gross, the hedge selector, fat-tail risk and scenario replays.

Correlation is not causation, so test the links several ways on the same six monthly series (oil, CPI, 10-year, stocks, VIX, gold), by regime. Python is canonical; the page renders the result (site/src/snap11.js or brain.json).
Command line.
Configuration: universe, risk limits and data settings, loaded from TOML.

Damodaran's two working tools, as he describes them: the implied equity risk premium (the discount rate that makes the index equal the present value of the cash it is expected to return), and narrative-to-numbers valuation (a story about a business turned into revenue growth, a target margin, reinvestment through a sales-to-capital ratio, a cost of capital that drifts to a mature level, a terminal growth no higher th
The data hub: every market-data source the engine can read, behind one interface, with a connection check.
Decision math: sizing a bet, scoring forecasts, and telling skill from luck.
Learning the brain's structure from the data, instead of assuming it.
The engine registry: every engine, what it reads, what it writes, and a manifest of the last run.
Noteworthy: an asymmetric-information feed scraper.

Field research (review revision 5): compare competing explanations of one observation, and pick the next piece of evidence that best separates them. Discrete Bayes; the page runs the same functions (site/src/field.js).
10-K and 10-Q analysis of the AI builders, straight from SEC XBRL facts.
Game theory for the book: who else is choosing, and what their best response does to ours.

Poker, haggling and private markets: the decision math that trading borrows, exact where it can be and simulated where it cannot. Python is canonical; site/src/labs.js runs the same functions on the page (tests/test_v14.py).

Prebuilt hedges for the book, each one switchable, sized, costed and run through the same seven 3-month scenarios as the solver (reasoner.SCENARIOS). The page runs the same arithmetic (site/src/hedgebook.js); tests/test_v11.py checks they agree.
JSON helpers shared by every report the page reads.

The labs: every claim a trader repeats, tested on the longest data the engine can read, with the statistics that keep a lucky backtest from passing for an edge. Python is canonical; the page renders labs.json (or snap14.js).
Free-data regime monitor: is the long Treasury hedging US growth stocks right now?
Market reads from the free FRED run: what moved, the price of insurance, and the plumbing.
Buildout as an MCP server: the engine's research, risk and reasoning as tools an assistant can call.
Market making and execution: the closed forms the Trading desks use, and estimators for the daily bars.
The mind: the brain and the engine as one graph, and a reasoning loop that runs on it.
Machine learning that a skeptical portfolio manager can audit: what it forecasts, how it was validated, how often it would have been fooled, and whether today looks like anything it has seen.

The concept layer of the mind: what an investor needs to know, as a typed graph. Each concept has a plain definition (our words), an optional formula, aliases a reader might type, and typed relations to other concepts, to measured series (s:...), to engine modules (e:...) and to voices topics (t:...). mind.py joins this with the atlas, the engine, the countries and the voices into one graph.
The decision loop: Observe, Orient, Decide, Act (Boyd), as one record the page renders and the journal can keep.
End-to-end run: data -> exposures -> regime -> hedge -> sizing -> risk -> stress -> backtest -> report.
Decision policies: one specification, used by the recommendation, its explanation and the backtest.
The reasoner: from evidence to a sized, constrained, explainable choice, and to what is worth learning next.
Original research on 155 years of public data, reproducible with one command:
Reinforcement learning for position sizing, judged out of sample.
Robust statistics for the brain's measured links: would the conclusion survive bad months, fat tails and autocorrelation?
Rates of change: how fast a market is moving toward a decision threshold, and whether it is speeding up.
Every data source the engine and the page read, in one registry (python -m buildout sources --out site/data).
Fundamental analysis from the filings themselves.
Run status for the page: which outputs exist, how fresh each one is, and the sanity checks it passed.
Technical analysis, built to be tested rather than believed.
The brain's reasoning: from what moved to why, what follows, what is wrong with the map, and what to look at next.
Fundamentals, accounting quality and what the market is pricing in, per position.

Voices: what legendary and current investors actually said about a question, arranged from extreme bear to extreme bull. Python is canonical; site/src/voices.js runs the same retrieval in the page (tests/test_v12.py holds them equal).
Daily backtester with explicit dollars: positions, cash, financing, trading costs.
Bond math: exact repricing, duration/convexity, and long-bond return proxies from FRED yields.
Treasury curve analytics from par yields: zero curve, forwards, carry and roll-down, futures DV01.
Factor exposures: exponentially weighted least squares, updated recursively (no lookahead).
Hedge sizing and evaluation. All hedge ratios are $ of hedge per $1 of book, applied the next day.
Performance statistics, including the probabilistic and deflated Sharpe ratios (Bailey and Lopez de Prado), which discount a backtest for luck and for how many variants were tried.
Black-Scholes with a continuous dividend yield, Greeks and implied volatility.
Stock-bond regime detection and shock classification.
Returns and factor construction.
Portfolio risk: covariance, risk contributions, concentration and diversification, VaR/CVaR (historical and FHS).
How much of a backtest would survive a different history, and how much is selection?
Signals and a walk-forward probabilistic model, evaluated honestly (calibration, not just hit rate).
Position sizing: volatility targeting, shrunk fractional Kelly, equal risk contribution, drawdown-constrained leverage, and rule-based trims.
Stress tests: replay historical episodes and price hypothetical factor shocks.
Volatility forecasting. Risk is far more predictable than return, so sizing leans on these.
Free fallback for corporate actions, used when Databento's adjustment factors are not on the account.
CSV fallback: a wide file of adjusted closes (first column date, one column per ticker).
Databento: split/dividend-adjusted daily closes for US equities and ETFs, and roll-adjusted CME Treasury futures returns.
SEC EDGAR XBRL: quarterly operating cash flow, capex, free cash flow and debt straight from filings.
FRED (St. Louis Fed): Treasury yields, breakevens, credit spreads, VIX, cash rates. Free, no key.
Minimal stdlib HTTP helper (no extra dependencies), with polite retries.
Kalshi public market data: prediction-market probabilities as macro features (Fed path, CPI, recession).
A screen on prices before they become returns. It flags; it never edits a price.
Parquet cache so paid data is pulled once and reused.
Synthetic market with KNOWN answers, used to prove the engine works before trusting it on real data.
The 10-month and 22 other moving-average rules on 156 years, with a stationary bootstrap, an SPA-style max test and a deflated Sharpe.
RSI, MACD, Bollinger, golden cross and 52-week-high signals tested against forward returns with Newey-West errors.
SMA, EMA, Wilder RSI, MACD, Bollinger bands and drawdown, the same arithmetic on the page.
CAPE, trailing P/E, dividend yield and the excess CAPE yield against 1- and 10-year real returns, with out-of-sample R squared.
Hamilton's two-state Markov switching model of monthly S&P 500 returns by EM, with the Kim smoother.
GARCH(1,1) by quasi maximum likelihood for Brent, WTI and gas, with tail indexes.
Engle-Granger cointegration of Brent and WTI with simulated p-values, the spread's half-life and z-score; gold/oil.
Lo-MacKinlay variance ratios against a random walk and against Working's averaging null.
Sell in May since 1871 and since 1950, and natural gas seasonality.
Every p-value from the labs in one table with Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections.
Expanding-window refits that only train on rows whose 12-month outcome had ended, plus an embargo.
28 purged splits of 8 time blocks and the probability that the in-sample winner misleads.
Forecast intervals from the models' own past errors, with their realised coverage.
The months most like today and what followed.
How far today sits from its nearest historical neighbours.
Fat tails, dependence, stability and correlation, each tested on the data.
The cost, delay, edge error or correlation at which each model's conclusion flips.
400 block-bootstrapped histories in which each decision is re-run.
Fat-tailedness in sample-size terms, for stocks, oil, gas and the VIX.
Whether the book's losses accelerate in the tail, with and without each hedge.
The discount rate that equates the index with its expected cash flows.
A story turned into growth, margin, reinvestment, cost of capital and failure risk.
Moving averages, RSI, MACD, Bollinger, ATR, ADX, stochastic, Ichimoku, Supertrend, SAR, OBV, money flow.
Each signal's edge on the asset's own history, Newey-West t and false-discovery control; weights shrink with evidence.
Annual statements from XBRL company facts, latest filing wins, tags recorded.
The three classic accounting scores, with unknown inputs marked unknown.
Offline reinforcement learning over trend, volatility, valuation and drawdown, walk-forward from 1940.
Credentials and reachability for every data source, with fallbacks per ticker.

The engine's latest research: the out-of-sample TLT hedge line and its band, the stock-bond regime, data checks, the reasoner's scenario probabilities and the brain's readings, each with its date and evidence label.

The MODEL book (not personal positions): weights, limits, the engine's risk summary when a book run exists, which holdings are the same bet, and the book's sensitivity to each root cause in the brain.

Run YOUR holdings (for example from Robinhood's MCP) through the same lens as the model book: weights, limit checks, concentration, which names are the same bet, sensitivity to each root cause, the gap to the model book, and the portfolio vector to score with evaluate_trade. For this call only: nothing is stored; cannot trade.

The engine's decision loop: what the data says (observe), what it means and what each price requires (orient), the solver, the hedge book and an action per position with its frameworks (decide), and proposals, what to watch and when to look again (act).

One holding's accounting quality, the 10-year growth its price requires (reverse DCF), how often companies that size achieved it (base rates), and the case the price is right and wrong. Override market value or beta to test.

Switch the prebuilt hedges (TLT, put spread, collar, gold, VIX calls, index short, semis short, trend cut, de-gross) on or off at chosen sizes: the book in every scenario, growth, worst case, cost, and the advisor's sets.

Ask the mind (one graph of about 2,600 nodes joining the brain, the engine, about 400 checked facts and papers, 267 verified quotes, 213 economies, the S&P 500 companies, the ML models and the tested assumptions) a question or claim. Returns what it recalled, the claim it weighed, the probability with a leave-one-family-out range, the evidence for and against with weights and sources (one row is t

The labs' tested trading claims on the longest data the engine reads: the 10-month trend rule with a bootstrap, max test and deflated Sharpe; RSI, MACD, Bollinger and golden-cross tests; CAPE and P/E against future returns out of sample; Markov regimes; GARCH; Brent-WTI cointegration; variance ratios; Sell in May; every p-value with Holm and BH corrections.

Exact decision math from the card room: poker equity (seeded Monte Carlo over a seven-card evaluator) and pot odds, Kelly sizing, risk of ruin, Rubinstein and Nash bargaining, the expected-surplus haggling offer, IRR, TVPI/DPI/RVPI, Kaplan-Schoar PME, the Takahashi-Alexander J-curve, and the convenience yield a commodity curve implies.

Machine learning on 155 years of data, judged the honest way: purged walk-forward skill against the historical mean (with a Diebold-Mariano test), the chance that picking the in-sample winner misleads (CPCV), conformal intervals with their realized coverage, permutation importance, calibration, today's forecasts, the nearest historical analogs and how unfamiliar today is.

Where the engine's models meet the real world: each model's assumptions with a live test (fat tails, dependence, structural breaks, the stock-bond correlation by regime, crisis correlation), the breakpoint at which each conclusion flips (trend costs and delay, Kelly across windows, the TLT hedge's correlation limit), Taleb's kappa, the fragility heuristic and 400 resampled worlds.

What a quant's backtested Sharpe is worth live: after trading costs, the out-of-sample or post-publication decay McLean and Pontiff measured, the deflated Sharpe ratio for the number of variants tried, and the minimum backtest length.

Damodaran's two tools: the implied equity risk premium (kind erp: level, cash_yield, growth, rf) and the narrative-to-numbers DCF (kind dcf: revenue, growth_high, margin_now, margin_target, sales_to_capital, wacc_start, wacc_mature, rf, p_fail...).

Technical analysis for one ticker: every indicator (moving averages, RSI, MACD, Bollinger, ATR, ADX, stochastic, Ichimoku, Supertrend, parabolic SAR, OBV, money flow), today's signals, support and resistance, Fibonacci, pivots, divergences, the trend template, relative strength, and an event study of each signal on the ticker's own history with false-discovery control.

A company's annual statements from its SEC filings, ratios (margins, ROIC, cash conversion, accruals, capex to depreciation, stock pay, leverage, growth and its acceleration, Rule of 40), Piotroski F, Altman Z'' and Beneish M scores, and flags.

The reinforcement-learning sizing agent (fitted Q iteration over trend, volatility, valuation and drawdown states): its out-of-sample record against holding and the trend rule, the deflated chance its edge is real, and today's exposure. Research only.
Which data sources (Databento, Yahoo, Stooq, SEC, Treasury, CFTC, FRED, GitHub mirrors) and credentials the engine can reach.

What legendary and current investors actually said about a question or claim, arranged from extreme bear (-2) to extreme bull (+2): verbatim quotes with speaker, date and source link from a verified library. Never generates a quote.

The whole brain: every monthly series the engine reads (equities, rates, inflation, energy, metals, grains, softs, currencies, and in the daily run credit, activity and money), links learned by graphical lasso with stability selection and LiNGAM orientation, joined with the judged concepts and the holdings. Trace a shock month by month to any node, or read a node.

How far to trust the brain: out-of-sample coverage of its 90% error bars (textbook against adaptive conformal), the stacked weights on five rival world models, and each measured link's robustness value to an unseen common cause.
Run the TLT hedge policy hedge.tlt.v2 on a stock-bond correlation path and a 36-month inflation reading.

Score a candidate portfolio (equity, TLT hedge, put spread, gold) on the reasoner's seven 3-month scenarios: certainty-equivalent growth, worst case, the loss limit, regret against the alternatives, and the best portfolio on the grid.
Write a structured, hashed order PROPOSAL against the model book and check it against the limits. Never executes: a person reviews it and acts elsewhere.

Score one decision's process (logged before, sized by rule, kill respected, two sources) and its luck quadrant, or a whole journal export: calibration, hit rate, alpha after beta and the process-outcome grid.

Compare competing explanations of one observation by Bayes' rule and rank the unchecked evidence by how much doubt it would remove (bits). Use a field case (leadtime, pipeline, credit) or supply your own.

What the data says about the brain's own assumptions: the causal order learned by DirectLiNGAM against the assumed order, and each measured link's path over time (Kalman smoother): latest value, 90% band, drift and sign changes.

Reason over the brain (34 nodes, about 110 links): which root causes explain the readings, what that implies for each holding and the book, which link is most to blame for the misfit, what to observe next, and doing versus seeing a value.
