signals.text: The deflated excess Sharpe over holding is -0.17 a year.
Acting on the same month inflates the Sharpe to 0.80: monthly averaging (Working 1960) flatters trend rules on averaged data.
signals.flip: Daily data that show the same gain.

signals.text: A trend rule cut the worst drawdown from -77% to -48% at a cost of about 1.4 points of return a year: protection that works, at a price.
signals.flip: A rule that costs more than it saves.

signals.text: Timing rules lowered risk but not return in 156 years: holding compounded faster (7.1% against 5.7% real).
signals.flip: A timing rule that beats holding on return after costs.

signals.text: Of the oscillator signals the labs tested, 11 of 24 pass at 5% after the false discovery rate correction.
signals.flip: Most of them passing on new data.

signals.text: Monthly RSI of the S&P 500 is 78 (overbought by the textbook); the labs find such readings weak on their own.
signals.flip: RSI back in the middle of its range.

signals.text: CAPE explains a share of ten-year real returns out of sample (OOS R squared 0.17); the excess CAPE yield does better (0.32).
signals.flip: A negative out-of-sample R squared at ten years.

signals.text: Over one year it explains almost nothing (OOS R squared 0.04): valuation is a decade tool, not a timing tool.
signals.flip: A one-year OOS R squared above 0.05.

signals.text: High valuations lower ten-year returns but say little about the next year.
Markov switching puts today's chance of the turbulent regime at 2% (calm regimes last about 33 months on average).
Calm regime (98% probability): manias tend to run while volatility is low.
Since 1950, November to April beat May to October (p = 0.007).
signals.flip: The gap vanishing in the next decade.

signals.text: On the full sample since 1871 it is weaker (p = 0.097), and the 1950 start is a choice made after seeing the data.
Monthly S&P 500 returns have kurtosis 23 (3 for a bell curve) and a tail index near 3.8: crashes are far more common than a normal model says.
signals.flip: Thin tails, which no long sample has shown.

signals.text: Brent $126.55 (2026-10-14) is +34% from its 200-day average of $94.7; the 50-day is above the 200-day.
Brent's GARCH volatility is 73% a year against a long-run 62%.
signals.flip: Volatility back to its long-run level.

signals.text: Brent-WTI is $24.64, 2.0 standard deviations wide; the pair is cointegrated with a half-life near 11 days, so the gap tends to close from the Brent side when the shock fades.
An ounce of gold buys 38 barrels of Brent (2026-09), more than in 94% of months since 1987: gold is dear against oil.
signals.flip: The ratio back near its median of 19.

signals.text: The 10-year Treasury yields 5.13% (Oct 21), high enough to pay for holding duration.
A 5.13% 10-year yield says the bond market does not think inflation is beaten.
With the 10-year at 5.13%, holding gold costs a high yield given up.
A 5.13% 10-year raises the interest bill on a large federal debt.
The 36-month stock-bond correlation is +0.15 (2026-09): bonds have been falling with stocks, a weak hedge.
37% of fund managers say they would move into bonds at a 6% 10-year (BofA, October; secondary report).
Global observed oil stocks are 509 million barrels below end-February (IEA).
Dated (physical) Brent near $134 against futures near $107: steep backwardation means barrels are short now.
Oil through the Strait of Hormuz recovered to 10.9 mb/d in September (IEA monthly estimate; daily tanker counts in early October were still far below pre-war): supply is coming back.
The IEA has world oil demand falling 2.6 mb/d in 2026: high prices are destroying demand.
Oil demand falling 2.6 mb/d is a sign of strain on the world economy.
The EIA expects Brent near $105 in Q4 2026 and $84 for 2027, well under spot.
If Brent falls toward the EIA's $105 for Q4 and $84 for 2027, energy inflation reverses.
Brent at $126.55 (Oct 14) keeps headline inflation up; the Fed hiked 25bp on September 16.
Brent at $126.55 is an oil shock; most past shocks of this size came before a slowdown.
The UAE left OPEC and OPEC+ on May 1: one big producer no longer bound by quotas (secondary report).
Managed money is net long only 40,574 WTI contracts (CFTC, Oct 13): speculators are not crowded in oil.
Central banks bought 863 tonnes of gold in 2025 and 289 in Q2 2026 (World Gold Council).
Central banks keep buying gold, a slow move away from dollar reserves.
Gold was $4,176 at end-September, -23% from its $5,405 record in January.
Magnificent 7 earnings are growing 33.2% in Q3 against 27.7% for the other 493 (FactSet): the spend is showing up in profits.
signals.flip: Hyperscaler earnings growth below the rest of the index.

signals.text: The biggest companies are out-earning the rest (33.2% against 27.7%): their weight is earned, for now.
signals.flip: Their earnings growth falling to the index's.

signals.text: Mag 7 earnings growth of 33.2% funds chip orders.
The growth leaders are delivering growth: Mag 7 earnings +33.2%.
AI took 82.7% of US venture dollars through Q3 2026 (PitchBook-NVCA): capital this concentrated in one theme has preceded busts before.
signals.flip: AI's share falling while revenue keeps rising.

signals.text: Venture funds from 2017 have returned only 0.31x their money in cash (median DPI, Carta): private marks are not yet cash.
82% of fund managers named long semiconductors the most crowded trade in July (BofA; secondary report).
signals.flip: The trade falling down the crowded list.

signals.text: Long semiconductors is the most crowded trade in the BofA survey.
signals.flip: Positioning unwinding without a fall in price.

signals.text: The ten largest stocks are 36.4% of the S&P 500 (June 30): an index fund is a concentrated bet.
signals.flip: Concentration falling as the rest catches up.

signals.text: With the top ten at 36.4% of the index, even indexers are concentrated; diversify beyond the cap-weighted index.
Margin debt is $1.48 trillion (FINRA, September), near June's record, after a 15.9% jump in two months.
signals.flip: Margin debt falling while prices hold.

signals.text: Borrowed money in stocks is near a record ($1.48 trillion).
Margin debt near a record means forced selling if prices drop.
Same-day (0DTE) options were a record 66.2% of S&P 500 options volume in July (Cboe).
Retail investors were about 21% of US stock volume in 2025 (secondary report).
Corporate insiders sold $77.6 billion of stock in the first half of 2026 (secondary report).
Fund managers held 3.9% cash in September (BofA; secondary report); low cash is the survey's own contrarian warning.
55% of S&P 500 members are above their 200-day average (secondary): participation is middling.
Buyers of fund stakes paid on average 87% of NAV in H1 2026, venture 79% and real estate 68% (Jefferies): private marks are above what cash buyers pay.
signals.flip: Secondary prices at or above NAV.

signals.text: Buyout distributions were 14% of NAV (Bain), well below the long-run pace: money is stuck in funds.
Continuation vehicles are 89% of GP-led secondaries: managers selling assets to themselves.
NAV loans are about $100 billion and growing: borrowing against fund portfolios, sometimes to pay distributions.
US PE exits were $102.6 billion in Q2 2026 (PitchBook), with IPOs reopening: the exit window is open.
Secondary volume hit $118 billion in H1 2026 (Jefferies): a deep market to sell into exists.
Only 25% of US active funds beat their passive peers over ten years (Morningstar, mid-2026).
75% of active funds trailed passive peers over ten years.
Active funds charge 0.57% on average against 0.10% for passive (Morningstar 2025): a certain drag.
Sharpe (1991): before costs, active investors as a group earn the market return, so after costs they must trail it.
signals.flip: New evidence on a longer sample.

The machine-learning ensemble expects +2.8% real over the next year against a historical +6.6%; its out-of-sample skill is -6.0%, so it counts for little.
Models put a 15% fall within a year at 28% against a base rate of 21%; their Brier skill out of sample is -11.6%.
signals.flip: Skill turning positive with the probability still above base.

signals.text: Purged walk-forward since 1940: the ensemble's skill at forecasting 12-month returns is -6.0% against the historical mean; the best single model, combination of one-variable forecasts, restricted, is +2.5%.
signals.flip: Positive skill on the next decade of data.

signals.text: The one model that beats the mean: averaging eight one-variable forecasts with Campbell and Thompson's sign restrictions earns +2.5% skill (Diebold-Mariano t 1.5), small and not yet significant, as Rapach, Strauss and Zhou found.
Across 28 combinatorial purged splits, the configuration that looked best in sample landed below the median out of sample 82% of the time.
Picking the in-sample winner misleads 82% of the time on this data.
Today's market sits further from its nearest historical months than 26% of months do: the models have seen conditions like these before.
Of the 8 months most like today (1998, 2000, 1996, 2018…), 4 were followed by a real loss over the next year.
Published anomalies earn about 58% less after publication and 26% less out of sample (McLean and Pontiff 2016).
Across 888 algorithms, backtest Sharpe ratios explained under 2.5% of live performance (Wiecki et al. 2016).
65% of 452 published anomalies fail a t of 1.96 when replicated (Hou, Xue and Zhang 2020).
Counterpoint: Jensen, Kelly and Pedersen find most factors do replicate across 93 countries.
None of the six high-turnover anomalies Novy-Marx and Velikov studied survives trading costs in basic form.
In August 2007 a standard quant strategy lost 6.85% in three days unlevered, about a quarter of capital at 8 to 1 (Khandani and Lo).
Lopez de Prado (2018): most machine-learning funds fail through leakage, overfitting and non-stationary data, not weak algorithms.
On two years of data, seven tries are enough for a strategy with no edge to show an in-sample Sharpe of 1 (Bailey et al.).
Monthly stocks had 23 moves beyond 3 standard deviations where a bell curve expects 5; a normal 1-in-100 month understates the real one by 30%.
A normal model understates the worst month in a hundred by 30%; size for the fat tail.
Taleb's kappa: 0.13 for monthly stocks and 0.34 for daily gas; gas needs about 73 observations to learn what 30 Gaussian ones would.
A 30% TLT sleeve only lowers the book's risk while the stock-bond correlation is below -0.09; the latest 36-month reading is +0.15.
The classic bond hedge assumes a negative stock-bond correlation; the data now break that assumption.
signals.flip: A negative correlation for a year.

signals.text: The trend rule cut the worst drawdown in 92% of resampled histories, but beat holding on Sharpe in only 55%.

signals.text: The trend rule's Sharpe gain survives costs up to 56 basis points a switch (about 1.3 switches a year) but not a four-month delay.
From any 30-year backtest, the Kelly fraction for stocks ranged from 1.4 to 8.0 times capital: the edge is too uncertain for full Kelly.
The 95/85 put spread helps until the index is down about 15% and then stops: losses accelerate again below it (Taleb-Douady test). Selling puts is fragile throughout.
Of 9 engine models, 4 rest on an assumption the data break today: value at risk and the sharpe ratio, the tlt hedge, machine-learning forecasts, black-scholes option prices.
